abstract: This lecture by Dr. Newborn covers osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) techniques including soft tissue, counterstrain, and myofascial release. It discusses appropriate referrals for OMT, emphasizing that somatic dysfunction in acute musculoskeletal issues is highly treatable, whereas chronic conditions require setting patient expectations and often multiple sessions. Practical demonstrations show how to apply soft tissue techniques to the thoracic, lumbar, and cervical spine, with attention to anatomical risks such as the vertebral artery. Key teaching points include the importance of targeting muscle (not skin), holding tension for 30–90 seconds, and using the Spurling's test before cervical work.
key_points: Soft tissue technique involves kneading muscles perpendicular to the spine or along the origin‑insertion plane until relaxation occurs.

Counterstrain is an indirect technique: identify the point of maximal tenderness, shorten the muscle, and hold for up to 90 seconds, then return to neutral without having the patient activate the muscle.
Appropriate OMT referrals are for musculoskeletal conditions with identifiable somatic dysfunction—acute problems are more responsive than chronic ones.
TART (tissue texture change, asymmetry, restriction of motion, tenderness) helps distinguish acute (boggy) from chronic (ropey/fibrotic) dysfunction.
OMT can effectively treat tension headaches, overuse injuries, and some acute rib or sciatic complaints, but not non‑musculoskeletal conditions or mechanical problems like herniated discs.
Chronic pain often requires home exercises and stretches; patient expectations should be set that improvement may take multiple visits.
Cervical soft tissue work requires awareness of the vertebral artery and nerve roots; a negative Spurling's test is recommended before treatment.
Soft tissue is very low‑risk; avoid rubbing the skin by engaging the muscle layer with thenar eminences or thumbs.
Stress‑related tension in the neck and shoulders is a common contributor to chronic myofascial pain that OMT can address.
The same soft tissue principles apply to cervical spine, but with gentler technique and attention to the vertebral artery course through the transverse foramina.
The suboccipital release targets the nuchal line, where the rectus capitis and obliquus capitis muscles attach.
The greater and lesser occipital nerves exit the skull at the nuchal line; tension here can cause nerve impingement and headache.
